concepts.reused_or_minted: minted, at the top level with no namespace, following the registry's own convention for enums (`index-state`, `indexer-node-state`, `cluster-access-credential-type` are all namespace-less). THIS IS THE THIRD STATE VOCABULARY THE ROUND ASKED ABOUT, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT MERGED WITH EITHER PROMOTED ENUM. Its two values are Paused and Active, both written as plain prose words with the word 'mode' after them ('the indexer goes into the Paused mode on that node', 'the indexer goes into Active mode again on that node'), and its subject is the indexer on one node - which is also the subject of promoted `indexer-node-state` (ready, pause, warmup, 'n mutations remaining'). 'Paused'/'pause' and 'Active'/'ready' are plausibly the same two states under two spellings, but THE PAGE NEVER SAYS SO and neither does any page in this batch, so merging them would be my inference presented as documentation. Minting it as a separate nameable thing is what lets phase 2 see that the corpus has two enums for one subject.

concepts.label: Runtime state of an individual index (Warmup / Active)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted, top-level for the same reason as `indexer-mode`. Its two values are `Warmup` and `Active`, both in backticks on this page, and its subject is an INDEX, not the indexer: 'these indexes remain in the `Warmup` state', 'the indexes remain in `Active` state'. That makes it collide with promoted `index-state` (scheduled for creation, deferred, building, pending, online, offline, abridged), which is the index-level enum and contains neither Warmup nor Active. So the corpus now has, for the two subjects 'an index' and 'the indexer on a node', two promoted enums and two undefined prose vocabularies, and no page reconciles any pair. Kept separate for the same reason as above: the reconciliation is not stated anywhere, so it is not extractable.

notable_absence.finding: I did NOT assert any relation between `indexer-mode`, `index-runtime-state`, promoted `indexer-node-state` and promoted `index-state`, because the page states no relation between them and no other page in this batch does either. That absence is the answer to the round's second question: THE STATE VOCABULARIES ARE NOT SETTLED BY THESE PAGES. What this page adds is not a reconciliation but a fourth vocabulary and one strong piece of evidence about its shape - the sentence 'the indexer goes into the Paused mode on that node. Although the indexes remain in `Active` state' proves that Paused and Active here belong to two DIFFERENT subjects (the indexer, and the indexes on it) and can hold simultaneously. That kills the simplest possible reconciliation, which would have been to treat Active/Warmup/Paused as one three-member enum: Active appears in both the index-level and the indexer-level sentences, so either it is one word for two states or the two vocabularies overlap in exactly one member. The page gives no definitions for any of the three words, no list of possible values, no statement of which component reports them, and no link to the UI or REST field where a user would see them. Second absence, related: `Warmup` here is capitalised and backticked as an index state, while promoted `indexer-node-state` has 'warmup' lowercase as a NODE state - same word, two subjects, and the promoted enum's own registry note already warns that this page's vocabulary is deliberately unpromoted and unmerged. Third absence, unrelated: the page never says what happens to a memory-optimized index when the snapshot on disk is itself lost or stale, though it stakes the whole recovery story on that snapshot; and it never states a memory-optimized equivalent of the standard mode's 'total size can be much bigger than memory' claim beyond the implicit one. Fourth: the page describes Plasma's LSS, cleaner, hole punching, Bloom filters and compression in detail and never once states a settings surface, key name or range for any of them except Bloom filters - so five tunables are documented as behaviour with no way to tune them.

The decisive detail is (b) versus (c): ONE storage setting value, 'standard', is implemented by TWO different engines depending on edition. A setting whose value maps one-to-many onto engines cannot be the same kind of thing as an engine. So the registry's round-16 note on `index:standard-storage` ('THE DOCS USE STORAGE ENGINE AT TWO LEVELS AND THIS RECORD IS THE UPPER ONE') is confirmed by the only page that documents both levels, and the ruling that engines belong in `storage-engine:` is vindicated.
